title: RNA motifs, RNA structure, and motif context analyzed by RNAanalyzer3

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Opened the Zenodo deposit metadata and file list (one 182 KB zip, 'rnaanalyzer-v1.0.5.zip', CC-BY-4.0, resource type 'Software') and the full GitHub file tree (66 entries: Perl CGI scripts, HTML/CSS, Dockerfiles, third-party licence texts; no data directory, no FASTA, no CSV/TSV). Unzipped the Europe PMC supplement (1.19 MB: 6 figure images plus one 27-page PDF) and extracted the PDF text: the only labelled examples anywhere are four tiny hand-curated validation sets printed as PDF tables (Supplementary Tables 8-11) and a summary confusion-matrix table (Supplementary Table 3) totalling roughly 313 sequences across all four motif modules. Also fetched the live web server's examples page: it links only to help pages, no downloadable dataset.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The description of what each rule-based scan does internally, the sequence-length limits (20,000 nt submission, 5,000 nt folding, 2,500 nt pseudoknot, 1,500 nt suboptimal folding), and the claim that validation used 'manually curated positives, random negatives, and random + intended mutations'. I did not run the web server.

a1_downloadable.note: Nothing that is a dataset is deposited. The Zenodo DOI resolves to a 182 KB zip of Perl/CGI source code tagged resource_type 'Software'; the supplement is figures plus a 27-page PDF. The tool's outputs are produced per-submission on the web server and are not archived anywhere downloadable.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no table with a label column. The only labelled items (motif present / absent) are typeset rows inside PDF Supplementary Tables 8-11; any training set would have to be built from scratch, e.g. by scraping Rfam or miRBase and running the web server to generate annotations.

a3_inputs_present.note: The PDF validation tables give NCBI accession numbers (e.g. NR_004430.4 for U1 snRNA) and short detected sub-sequences, not full input sequences, so every input would need a database lookup.

a4_units_stated.note: Not really applicable: the outputs are yes/no motif calls and standard metrics (sensitivity, specificity, precision), whose formulas are spelled out on page 8 of the supplement.

a5_enough_rows.note: Counted from Supplementary Table 3's confusion matrices: iron-responsive element 19 true positives + 210 true negatives + 5 false positives + 0 false negatives = 234; AU-rich element 23; trans-splicing 35; Sm-site (small nuclear RNA protein-binding motif) 21. About 313 labelled sequences in total, split across four unrelated tasks, versus the ~400 minimum for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Everything that exists (182 KB code zip, 1.26 MB PDF) fits trivially; size was never the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The counts I extracted from the supplement PDF are self-consistent with the paper's text, which explicitly calls these 'targeted validation' sets 'rather than establishing a large-scale benchmark'.

a8_label_provenance.note: The negatives are synthetic by construction: 'matched loop/bulge/stem mutants' and 'random mRNA sequence'. Those negatives were generated by mutating exactly the positions the rule-based detector inspects, so a model trained on them would be learning the detector's rule, not biology.

existing_models.name: RNAanalyzer3 itself (rule-based motif scanner, not a learned model)
existing_models.score_and_split: Supplementary Table 3, on its own hand-made validation sets with no held-out split: iron-responsive element sensitivity 1.00 / specificity 0.98 / precision 0.79; AU-rich element 1.00 / 0.85 / 0.77; trans-splicing 0.67 / 0.74 / 0.57; Sm-site 1.00 / 0.38 / 0.33.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The authors state the Sm-site module 'still reports any U-rich sequences' (precision 0.33) and that trans-splicing detection is the weakest module; they explicitly decline to claim a large-scale benchmark.

backbone.name: RNA-FM (an RNA language model trained on ~23 million non-coding RNA sequences)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would suffice for a few hundred short sequences, but there are not enough sequences to fit a head.
backbone.licence: Open, but irrelevant given there is no dataset.

integration.partner_dataset: Rfam (a database of RNA families with covariance models) and miRBase (a microRNA catalogue), both of which the web server links out to
integration.join_key: Rfam family accession / NCBI nucleotide accession
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: One could ask whether a pretrained RNA language model recovers hand-written motif rules better than the rules themselves, but that project would be built entirely on Rfam, not on this paper, which contributes no data to it.

controls.positive_control: The 10 canonical iron-responsive elements listed in Supplementary Table 8 are textbook cases any detector must recover.
controls.negative_control: The paper's own negatives are point mutants of the positives plus random messenger RNA, which is a weak and circular negative set.
controls.external_validation: Rfam and miRBase exist as independent sources, but the paper itself provides no second set.

honest_claim_h3: Using only what this paper deposits, a model could claim nothing beyond 'it reproduces four hand-written regular-expression-style motif rules on the ~313 sequences the authors chose to illustrate them with'.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use an RNA sequence to predict which regulatory motifs it contains and where they sit in the folded structure.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on RNA sequences labelled with motif presence. This paper supplies about 313 such labelled sequences, printed inside a PDF, spread across four different motif types.
plain_idea.predict: Presence and position of regulatory motifs (iron-responsive element, AU-rich element, trans-splicing leader, Sm-site). The 'true answer' here comes from the authors' own rule-based scanner plus manual curation, not from an experiment.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: RNA biologists hunting regulatory elements in new transcripts would use a learned motif finder that tolerates degenerate matches better than fixed rules; but this paper supplies none of the data needed to build one.

ml_idea: The only project this paper supports would be distilling its four rule-based motif detectors into a learned model, trained on ~313 PDF-table sequences whose negatives are mutants of the positives. That is circular by construction and far too small. A real version of this task (learn RNA regulatory motifs with a pretrained RNA language model, held out by RNA family) would be built on Rfam and miRBase and would not use this paper at all.

effort.compute_note: Sizes are measured, not estimated: 182 KB code zip and a 1.26 MB PDF. No modelling estimates are meaningful because there is no dataset.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: List the Zenodo deposit's files (one API call). Seeing resource_type 'Software' and a single 182 KB source zip kills this in under a minute.

verdict_reason: A web server tool paper with no dataset: the deposit is 182 KB of Perl source code, and the only labelled examples are ~313 sequences typeset in PDF tables, with synthetic mutant negatives. Fails A1, A2, A3, A5 and A8.
